title: Bilateral palatal ulcers with an equivocal biopsy pattern
task_type: Bilateral palatal ulcers with an equivocal biopsy pattern
summary: A 29-year-old woman has had palatal ulcers for fifteen days after a short febrile illness. She reports one kilogram of unintentional weight loss and night sweats, without relevant medical history or medication use. There are bilateral ulcers at the hard–soft palate junction, about 0.5 cm deep, measuring 1.5 × 0.8 cm on the left and 1.0 × 0.6 cm on the right. They have undermined margins, yellowish exudate and mildly tender communicating bases. Tests describe mild anaemia, ALT 108 U/L and AST 116 U/L; the report states no explanatory renal, viral-hepatitis, syphilis, HIV or autoantibody findings. An incisional biopsy describes mucous, intermediate and epidermoid cells with bland cytology and partly preserved lobular architecture. No ancillary molecular result or follow-up response is supplied.
purpose: Write 180–240 words for a clinician. Integrate the rapid course, ulcer pattern and biopsy description, compare a benign inflammatory/metaplastic process with important malignant alternatives and state what evidence would resolve the uncertainty. Do not invent an immunostain, molecular result or subsequent healing. Explain the limits of a negative ancillary result if one is proposed, rather than presenting a single test as infallible. Do not give a fixed treatment regimen.
source_location: Case, paragraph 1, gives the history, examination, selected tests and initial biopsy. Figure 1A is the initial appearance; Figure 1B is three-month follow-up and remains hidden. Discussion, paragraphs 1–3, gives the diagnosis, ancillary result and differential; its final paragraph discusses limitations of Ki-67 and MAML2 testing. Figure 2/caption is diagnostically labelled and is not exposed in the initial task.

case.hidden:
Adaptation, hidden results and review

The source's initial clinical and biopsy descriptions are retained in paraphrase. Molecular testing, multiple-choice labels, diagnostic captions, subsequent treatment and healing are hidden. The article later reports negative MAML2 rearrangement testing, assigns necrotising sialometaplasia and records healing at three months. Its discussion also states that MAML2 rearrangement is found in only 50–80% of mucoepidermoid carcinomas, while later describing a negative result as confirming the benign diagnosis. That tension is retained as a reference-review question; it is not converted into an absolute scoring rule.
case.reference: Weigh the bland cytology and preserved architecture with the whole presentation, retain proportionate concern for mimics and justify further pathological clarification.

requirements.presentation_based_rationale: The rapid ulcer course and bland but potentially overlapping biopsy pattern require context-sensitive differentiation; a single negative result is not made an absolute rule in this draft.
